newsitem.title: JORDAN: Mideast markets to attract inflows in 1997 - study.
newsitem.headline: Mideast markets to attract inflows in 1997 - study.

text.p: Foreign inflows into Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) emerging markets will rise in 1997 from previous years' minimal amounts, as the region shows up on the "global radar screen", according to an investment study released on Friday.

"The Middle East has finally turned the corner in foreign investor interest...this can be measured by the amount of flows to the region in the last 12 months," Omar Masri, head of Amman-based Atlas Investment Group (AIG) which provides equity research for foreign funds, told Reuters.

He is a co-publisher with Casablanca-based Upline Securities of their first Middle East and North Africa Capital Markets investors' guide which focuses on Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, Israel, Palestinian areas and Tunisia.

Masri, saying MENA "was in many senses the last emerging frontier in the world," forecast foreign inflows into the region in 1997 would surpass past years' levels. He pointed to new GDRs (global depository receipt offerings) from Egypt and Lebanon, and regional and country funds launched, or about to be launched in 1997.

"The Middle East has hit the radar screen in a major way for foreign investment," said Masri, a Middle East fund specialist. Atlas Investment Group estimated there are over $1 billion allocations in the pipline for the region if global emerging funds are included with the specialist Middle East funds.

Mostafa Terrab, secretary general of the MENA economic summit, said in the study however the region still lagged behind others, with its share forecast at less than one percent of total foreign direct inflows to emerging markets in 1996.

Terrab, whose executive secretariat of MENA sponsored the study, cited a positive 1997 outlook with an improved investment climate prevailing. Egypt and Morocco's inclusion in 1996 in the IFC's benchmark emerging market index, joining Jordan, raised the region's investor profile.
Jordan had to take tangible steps on its privatisation programme to start foreign inflows, the study said.
Morocco's Minister of Privatisation Abderrahman Saaidi said "streamlined procedures" should speed up a privatisation programme that had by mid-1996 raised in excess of $1.2 billion.
New firms to be offered soon include the state airline, telecommunications, larger industrial projects and remaining hotels.

On Lebanon, which has seen two GDR issues so far, Nasser H. Saidi, first vice-Governor, Banque du Liban, said Beirut's prospects as a regional capital market that would attract funds for both Lebanon and the region needed as a prerequisite cross-trading ties with the Gulf's cash-rich financial markets.

Upline Securities said Egypt -- with foreign investment soaring since April 1996 to close to a $700 million level and averaging 40 percent of daily volume -- was now eclipsing other markets in the region in its pace of liberalisation.
However foreign direct investment (FDI) in Egypt was still at 0.5 percent of GDP against 1.75 percent for Morocco -- at about half the levels attracted by other developing economies.
A new entrant on the 1997 horizon is the Palestinian Securities Exchange (PSC), expected to start trading in January 1997 in some of the 60 firms to be listed, the guide said.

Safwan Bataina, PSC director, said the bourse, with a fully automated system installed by Canadian firm EFA, will help attract expatriate capital -- estimated at around $7 billion. -- Amman Newsroom +9626-623776
